sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Esotropia (ET) is a form of strabismus where the visual axes intersect in front of the object of regard. It is categorized by onset (congenital vs. acquired), frequency (constant vs. intermittent), and mechanism (accommodative vs. non-accommodative). Precise diagnosis is critical as it may be the presenting sign of life-threatening pathology such as retinoblastoma or intracranial tumors.

sections.title: Infantile Esotropia Syndrome (IES)
content: Onset: Within the first 6 months of life.
Angle: Usually large (>30 Prism Diopters) and stable.
Refraction: Usually normal for age (approx +1.50D).
Cross-fixation: Patient looks left with right eye and right with left eye.
Latent Nystagmus: Jerk nystagmus appearing when one eye is covered.
Dissociated Vertical Deviation (DVD): Upward drift of the non-fixing eye (found in 50-90%).
Inferior Oblique Overaction (IOOA): Frequent late finding.

rows: ET greater at near than distance
Significant ET at both, worse at near
Residual ET remains after full correction

sections.title: Ocular Examination Protocol
content: Step 1: History (Onset, frequency, family history).
Step 2: Visual Acuity (Fix and Follow, CSM, or Snellen/LEA).
Step 3: Cover/Uncover and Alternate Cover Test (Prism neutralization).
Step 4: Ocular Motility (Versions/Ductions, look for IOOA or A/V patterns).
Step 5: Cycloplegic Refraction (1% Atropine or 1% Cyclopentolate mandatory).
Step 6: Dilated Fundus Exam (Rule out sensory causes like Retinoblastoma).

sections.title: Sensory Esotropia Red Flags
content: Leukocoria (White pupillary reflex)
Optic Atrophy or Hypoplasia
Macular Scars (e.g., Toxoplasmosis)
Retinoblastoma (Must exclude in ALL new cases)
Dense Cataract

rows: Prominent epicanthal folds; symmetrical Hirschberg reflex.
Limited abduction, globe retraction/narrowing of palpebral fissure on adduction.
Recent onset, limited abduction, diplopia (if old enough), head turn.
Large angle ET with limited abduction and jerk nystagmus.

content.explanation: AC/A = (Δ1 - Δ2) / D. Where Δ1 is original deviation, Δ2 is deviation with lens, and D is power of lens used.

sections.title: Surgical Management: Infantile ET
content: 1. Stabilization: Ensure amblyopia is treated first.
2. Procedure Selection: Bilateral Medial Rectus (BMR) Recession is gold standard.
3. Dosing: 5mm for 20-25PD; 6mm for 30-35PD; 7mm for 45-50PD.
4. Associated Patterns: Address Inferior Oblique (Myectomy) if OAIO is present.
5. Timing: Ideally before 2 years of age to maximize binocular potential.

sections.title: Post-Operative Complications
content: Slipped or Lost Muscle (Surgical emergency)
Consecutive Exotropia (Overcorrection)
Globe Perforation
Anterior Segment Ischemia (Risk if >2 muscles/eye)
Suture Granuloma or Tenon's Prolapse

sections.title: Special Form: Acute Acquired Comitant ET
content: Swan Type: Following occlusion/loss of vision.
Burian-Franceschetti Type: Idiopathic, large angle, no refractive error.
Bielschowsky Type: Found in uncorrected myopes due to near work.
NEURO ALERT: Acute ET can be a sign of cerebellar tumor (Chiari Malformation).

sections.title: The ELIS Trial & Timing of Surgery
sections.content: The Early vs. Late Infantile Strabismus (ELIS) study suggests that surgery performed before age 2, specifically between 6 months and 2 years, results in better stereopsis and gross binocularity compared to delayed surgery, though re-operation rates may be higher.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Board Exam
content: Always check for a 'V' or 'A' pattern; 'V' is often IOOA, 'A' is often SOOA.
Prism Adaptation Test (PAT): Used to identify patients who 'eat' prism before surgery.
Monofixation Syndrome: A common 'success' state after ET surgery (small angle, central scotoma, peripheral fusion).
Sensory ET in adults: If sudden onset, think intracranial pressure.

content.explanation: D: Diminished Abduction, U: Up/Down shoots, A: Adduction causes globe retraction, N: Narrowing of fissure, E: Esotropia in primary position.

sections.title: Investigations: Ancillary Testing
content: Worth 4-Dot Test: Assess for suppression or diplopia.
Stereopsis Testing: Titmus Fly or Randot (IES usually has no stereopsis).
Hess Screen / Lancaster Red-Green: Useful for paralytic ET.
Neuroimaging (MRI/CT): Mandatory if ET is associated with neurological signs, ataxia, or papilledema.

sections.title: Summary of Success Criteria
content: Primary Success: Orthotropia within 10 PD of central alignment.
Functional Success: Restoration of gross stereopsis (e.g., 200-400 arc sec).
Cosmetic Success: Deviation not noticeable by casual observers.

sections.content: An exhaustive clinical guide to Esotropia, a manifest inward deviation of the visual axes and the most common form of childhood strabismus in the UK. This poster covers the classification, assessment, and management of accommodative, non-accommodative, and secondary esodeviations.

sections.title: Core Definitions & Classification
content: Definition: Esotropia is a manifest inward deviation of the visual axes.
Prevalence: It is the commonest form of childhood strabismus in the UK.
Primary (1°): Classified as accommodative or non-accommodative.
Secondary (2°): Most commonly due to poor vision (sensory deprivation).
Consecutive: Occurs after surgery for an exodeviation.

sections.title: Essential Clinical Assessment
content: Step 1: Perform full refraction.
Step 2: Conduct a full ophthalmic examination.
Step 3: Address amblyopic risk if appropriate (consider patient age).
Step 4: Rule out underlying pathology at the outset.

sections.title: Pathology Alert: Rule Out At Outset
content: Intraocular tumour (e.g., Retinoblastoma)
Cataract
Other underlying organic pathology

branches: Neurological Link: Accommodation and convergence are neurologically linked.
AC:A Ratio: Measure of accommodative convergence per unit of accommodation; varies between individuals.
Mechanism: Young, uncorrected hypermetropes accommodate to see clearly, triggering convergent drive.
High AC:A Ratio: Particularly likely to develop esotropia at near vision.
Presentation: Usually presents between 1 and 5 years of age.
Types: May be refractive or non-refractive (abnormally high AC:A), often with overlap.

rows: Fully corrected for distance and near by hypermetropic correction (+2 to +7D).
Only partially corrected by full hypermetropic correction.
Normal Binocular Single Vision (BSV) if corrected.
BSV absent or limited with ARC (Abnormal Retinal Correspondence).
Often intermittent initially (e.g. with fatigue, illness).
Full hypermetropic correction; allow 12wk for spectacle adaptation; treat amblyopia.
Full hypermetropic correction; treat amblyopia; consider surgery for BSV potential or cosmesis.

sections.title: Non-Refractive: Convergence Excess
content: Mechanism: Esotropia for near due to high AC:A ratio.
Distance Status: Ortho- or esophoric for distance.
BSV: dBSV for near, normal BSV for distance.
Refraction: Usually hypermetropic.
Treatment 1: Treat any associated hypermetropia or amblyopia.
Treatment 2: Consider orthoptic exercises or executive bifocal glasses.
Treatment 3: Surgery (bilateral MR recession and/or posterior fixation sutures) or miotics.

sections.title: Infantile Esotropia (Congenital)
content: Definition: Commonest non-accommodative esotropia; presents before 6 months of age.
Clinical Signs: Large angle (>30Δ) and alternating fixation (low risk of amblyopia).
Potential: Poor Binocular Single Vision (BSV) potential.
DVD: Dissociated Vertical Deviation - incomitant tendency for occluded eye to elevate and extort, resolving on uncovering.
LN: Latent Nystagmus - horizontal, conjugate jerk nystagmus on occluding one eye, fast phase away from covered eye (ACE).
IOOA: Inferior Oblique Overaction - hyperdeviation in adduction, greatest in field of IO.

sections.title: Management of Infantile Esotropia
content: Treat associated amblyopia (e.g., occlusion of better eye if not freely alternating).
Correct hypermetropia if >2D.
Surgery: Aims for ocular alignment.
Additional Surgery: May be required for significant IOOA or DVD.

rows: Increased chance of BSV (Simonsz et al. 2005; Birch et al. 2000).
Less accurate preoperative measurements (Prism Cover Test - PCT).
BSV from early Sx is poor quality/functionally not important.
Proceeding without stable PCT does not affect outcome (Lueder et al. 2008).
BSV can be achieved even after late surgery (Murray et al. 2007).

sections.title: Other Non-Accommodative Types
content: Basic Esotropia: Constant ET for near and distance; treat surgically.
Near Esotropia (Non-accommodative convergence excess): ET for near, ortho-/esophoria for distance; normal AC:A ratio. Treatment: Surgical (MR > LR).
Distance Esotropia (Divergence insufficiency): Esophoria/small ET for near, larger ET for distance; poor fusional divergence. NB: Exclude bilateral VI palsy. Treat with orthoptic exercises initially.
Cyclic Esotropia: Rare, periodic (e.g., alternate days); may proceed to constant esotropia.
Nystagmus Blockage & Cianca Syndrome: Large angle infantile ET, nystagmus increases on abduction, head turn towards fixing eye.

sections.title: Secondary Esotropias & Pseudoesotropia
content: Sensory Deprivation: Secondary to unilateral/bilateral decreased Visual Acuity (dVA).
Divergence Paralysis: Secondary to tumour, trauma, or stroke. Deviation remains constant or decreases on lateral gaze (unlike VI palsy).

Convergence Spasm: Intermittent, associated with blurred vision (pseudomyopia) and pupillary miosis. Ductions normal without miosis. Exclude upper midbrain pathology; often non-organic. Treat with cycloplegia.
Pseudoesotropia: Various conditions mimicking esotropia (see Table 17.6).
